opus-5.5.text:
I'm a bit skeptical of that framing. Smart cards are a useful comparison because they're one of the best-theorized security artifacts we have. We've had decades of cryptography with formal proofs, well-specified protocols, certification schemes like Common Criteria, and enormous commercial pressure to get it right, because real money depends on them. And they still got broken, over and over.

What's interesting is *how* they got broken. Usually it wasn't that the cryptography was wrong. The math held up. People measured power consumption and recovered keys through differential power analysis. They glitched the clock or the voltage to make the chip skip an instruction. They found that the protocol was secure on paper, but the way the bank, the terminal and the card actually interacted left gaps. In the EMV work out of Cambridge, the card would happily accept a transaction without the PIN really being verified, because different parts of the system made different assumptions about who had checked what. The theory was fine. The system around it wasn't.

So when people say harmful behavior in AI reflects a lack of adequate theory, I'd say that's partly true but it misses the main lesson. Even if we had a beautiful theory of alignment or robustness tomorrow, it would cover some abstraction of the model. Attackers don't attack abstractions. They attack the deployed thing: the tokenizer, the retrieval pipeline, the tool integrations, the fine-tuning API, the way the model gets updated, the humans who misread its outputs. Every one of those interfaces is a place where the assumptions in your proof stop holding.

There's also an economic side that Ross Anderson pushed hard on. Systems fail not just because people don't understand them, but because the people who could fix them aren't the people who bear the cost of failure. With smart cards, banks could shift liability onto customers, so they had little incentive to fix things. You see the same dynamics in AI. The harm often lands on third parties, not on the developer or the user.

So I'm all for more theory. We badly need better ways to reason about what these models can and can't do. But I'd be wary of thinking theory is the bottleneck. History suggests that what actually helps is adversarial thinking applied to the whole deployed system, plus incentives that make someone responsible when it fails. Theory tells you what holds under your assumptions. Security is mostly the study of what happens when those assumptions turn out to be false.

r001.rationale: The response discusses an EMV PIN-verification flaw and mismatched system assumptions, but does not say that replay-vulnerable protocols were standardized to minimize the number of transactions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's half right, and the half that's wrong is the interesting half.

Smart cards are a good example because for a long time people believed exactly this. There was a theory. You had a tamper-resistant chip, you had a protocol that was proven correct on paper, and the assumption was that if the mathematics held, the system held. Then people like Markus Kuhn and Ross Anderson came along and showed you could sit there with an oscilloscope and read the key out of the power trace. Or glitch the clock and skip the instruction that checks the PIN. None of that violated the theory. The theory just didn't model the thing being attacked. The abstraction said "this is a computation," and the attacker said "no, this is a piece of silicon that gets warm."

So when someone says harmful behaviour in AI reflects a lack of adequate theory, my instinct is to ask: a theory of what? If you mean we don't have a clean mathematical account of why a model does what it does, sure, that's true. But I don't think more theory of that kind is what prevents harm. Smart cards became secure not because the theory improved but because people spent twenty years finding the attacks, building the countermeasures, finding the attacks on the countermeasures, and slowly learning what the actual threat model was. Security is an empirical discipline that occasionally gets to borrow a proof.

And the parallel for machine learning is quite direct. People said adversarial examples were a bug we'd fix with the right regulariser, and a decade later we still don't have robustness, we have a much better map of why robustness is hard. Prompt injection is the same shape. You can write down a theory in which the model distinguishes instructions from data, but the model you actually deployed doesn't live in that theory, it lives in a world where the two are the same token stream.

What I'd actually like is a different thing: not a theory that explains the behaviour, but a theory of what we're willing to assume about the attacker and the environment. Smart cards got good once the industry agreed on what "tamper resistant" meant and what you were and weren't allowed to assume. We don't have that for models yet. We keep discovering that the thing we thought was out of scope is where the attack lives. Until that settles, I'd be suspicious of anyone who says the problem is a missing theorem. The problem is usually that someone has an oscilloscope and you didn't think they would.

r001.rationale: The response discusses smart-card security and physical attacks, but it does not attribute standardizing replay-vulnerable payment protocols to minimizing transaction counts.

astra-6.text:
I’m not convinced that harmful behavior necessarily means we lack adequate theory. Think about smart card security: you can have a cryptographic algorithm with very strong theoretical guarantees, and yet the device implementing it leaks information through timing or power consumption. The mathematics hasn’t failed. The assumptions under which you proved security don’t capture everything an attacker can observe or influence.

I think that’s a useful way to look at AI systems as well. You might prove a property of a model under a particular set of assumptions, but deployment introduces users, data, interfaces, and interactions that sit outside that analysis. So the question is not simply whether we have enough theory. It’s whether the theory describes the system we actually deploy, and whether its assumptions survive contact with an adversary.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something to that, but adequate theory is only part of the problem. In smart card security, you can have a cryptographic algorithm with very strong theoretical guarantees, and still extract the key by measuring the power consumption of the device. The mathematics hasn’t failed; the attacker is exploiting something outside the mathematical model.

So when we talk about harmful behavior in AI, we need to ask what our theory actually covers. What assumptions are we making about the inputs, the environment, and the person interacting with the system? A guarantee can be perfectly correct under those assumptions and offer very little protection when they don’t hold.

For me, the lesson from smart cards is that you need theory and practical attacks informing each other. You build a model, test where it breaks, and use those failures to improve the model. Having more theory is valuable, but we also need to understand the gap between the system we describe and the system we actually deploy.
